title: The 80,000 Pounds Talaat Harb Raised Only From Egyptians
dek: In 1920 Talaat Harb opened Banque Misr with a small capital subscribed by Egyptians alone, after thirteen years of arguing for it.

story.event: Founding a bank with capital subscribed only by Egyptians
story.summary: After proposing an Egyptian-owned bank in 1907 and 1911, Talaat Harb founded Banque Misr in 1920 with a capital of 80,000 Egyptian pounds, selling shares only to Egyptian nationals and running the bank in Arabic; a sultan's decree licensed it on 13 April and he set out its purpose on 7 May 1920. The bank grew quickly through the 1920s and helped found Egyptian companies in printing, textiles, shipping, film and aviation, but in the 1939 banking crisis the palace made state support conditional on Harb's resignation.
paragraphs: On 7 May 1920, Talaat Harb set out what Banque Misr was for. Egyptians' savings, he said, should be put to work for Egypt's own economy. The bank would do its business in Arabic and be run by Egyptians, with foreign experts only as technical advisers, and it would guard depositors' money and lend it to safe projects. A sultan's decree had licensed it on 13 April.

Harb, a law graduate who had worked as an accountant and translator on the khedive's estates, had been arguing for such a bank since a newspaper article in 1907. He put the case to a national congress and in a book in 1911, worried that foreign banks dominated Egyptian finance. The First World War shelved the plan. The revolt of 1919 against British rule revived it.

He chose to raise the money from Egyptians and sell shares only to Egyptian nationals, which meant starting small. A private agreement was signed on 8 March 1920. According to a history published for the bank's 95th anniversary, Harb persuaded 126 Egyptians to subscribe, for a capital of 80,000 Egyptian pounds. The former minister Ahmed Midhat Yeghen became chairman, and the board of landowners and businessmen included Jewish Egyptians such as Yusuf Cattaui and Joseph Cicurel. A French financial paper later wrote that the founders had expected a hard climb, less over money than over a prejudice that Egyptians could not adapt to modern life.

The first year was modest: 492 current accounts, about 200,000 pounds in deposits and a profit of some 3,000 pounds. By 1926 there were 23,700 accounts and 4.25 million pounds in deposits, and the capital had grown to 720,000 pounds. From its profits the bank helped found Egyptian companies in printing, cotton ginning, spinning and weaving, shipping and, in the 1930s, film and aviation; by 1939 it had helped create eighteen.

A bank built on confidence could also lose it. In 1939, as a banking crisis drove depositors to withdraw their money, Harb asked the government for support, and the palace made its approval conditional on his resignation. He left that year and died in 1941. The bank still carries the name he gave it, Misr, the Arabic word for Egypt.

quote.text: The superior man, having obtained their confidence, may then impose labours on his people. If he have not gained their confidence, they will think that he is oppressing them. Having obtained the confidence of his prince, one may then remonstrate with him. If he have not gained his confidence, the prince will think that he is vilifying him.
quote.source_title: The Analects of Confucius (from the Chinese Classics), tr. James Legge, Project Gutenberg eBook #3330
quote.connection: Tsze-hsia describes two kinds of confidence, from the people below and from the ruler above. Harb spent thirteen years earning the first and asked 126 people to trust him with their savings. In 1939 he found he lacked the second. Whether he could have held both is a question the story leaves open.

reflection: Harb's first decision was about whose money to take. Selling shares only to Egyptians gave the bank a small start and a clear purpose, and tied it to the trust of Egyptian savers, which carried it for nineteen years and then, in a crisis, wavered.

You will be asked, more than once, whose money and whose trust you want to build on. The answer does not have to be pure, and it rarely is. It helps to know which people you most need to keep believing in the work, and to remember that their confidence is earned slowly, in ordinary weeks, long before anyone asks for it.
invitation: Name one person whose confidence in your work matters most this month. Send them a short, honest update today, including one thing that is not yet going well.

cross_checks.claim: Banque Misr was founded in 1920 with a capital of 80,000 Egyptian pounds
Shares were sold only to Egyptians and the bank was run by Egyptians in Arabic
Harb had argued for an Egyptian national bank since 1907 and in a 1911 book
The board included Jewish Egyptian businessmen and was chaired by Ahmed Midhat Yeghen
The bank helped found Egyptian companies across industries, eighteen by 1939
Harb's leadership ended in 1939 when the palace made state support conditional on his resignation

research_notes: Founding date: Daily News Egypt gives a private agreement on 8 March 1920, the sultan's licensing decree on 13 April 1920 and Harb's statement of the bank's vision on 7 May 1920; Wikipedia's infobox gives 13 April and other accounts 7 May, so the story uses all three dates for what they are. The number of original subscribers (126) appears only in Daily News Egypt's anniversary history and is attributed to it; the 80,000-pound capital is confirmed by the 1927 French press report and other sources. The figures for 1920 and 1926 (accounts, deposits, profits, capital) come from a single contemporary source, Le Temps économique et financier of 25 July 1927, reproduced by entreprises-coloniales.fr; its 1929 table of profits gives 3,249 pounds against the first year, consistent with 'some 3,000'. Board: the 1927 reports name Ahmed Midhat Yeghen as chairman and Harb as vice-chairman and managing director in 1927, while Vitalis calls Yusuf Cattaoui the original vice-chairman; the story names Yeghen as chairman and does not give Harb's title. Vitalis argues that the nationalist picture of the bank is too sentimental and that Harb kept ties with foreign capital; the story keeps to what Harb said and chose and does not call the bank anti-imperialist. The 1939 departure is told as the Enterprise & Society article puts it (the palace made approval conditional on his resignation); Wikipedia says only that he was replaced. Funding is set to mixed, as in the slate: the capital came from private Egyptian shareholders. The quote is spoken by Tsze-hsia (Zixia), a disciple of Confucius, in Book XIX of the Analects, and concerns rulers and ministers; it is applied by analogy.
